paragraphs: To lay out the general cause of these differences, we need to distinguish government from its principle, just as we distinguished earlier between the State and the Sovereign.

The body of magistrates can have more members or fewer. We said earlier that the relation of the Sovereign to the subjects grows as the people grows more numerous. By a clear analogy, the same holds for the relation of the government to the magistrates.
But the total force of the government is always the State’s force, and so it never varies. The more of it the government spends on its own members, the less it has left for the whole people.
So the more magistrates there are, the weaker the government. Since this principle is fundamental, we must work to make it clear.

In the person of a magistrate we can tell apart three essentially different wills. First, the private will of the individual, which aims only at his own advantage. Second, the common will of the magistrates, which looks solely to the advantage of the prince. We can call it the corporate will; it is general with respect to the government and particular with respect to the State, of which the government is a part. Third, the will of the people, or the sovereign will, which is general both with respect to the State seen as the whole and with respect to the government seen as a part of that whole.

In a perfect act of legislation, the individual or particular will should count for nothing. The corporate will of the government should hold a very minor place. The general or sovereign will should therefore always prevail, and be the sole guide for all the rest.

The natural order, by contrast, works the other way: these different wills grow more active the more concentrated they are. So the general will is always the weakest, the corporate will comes second, and the individual will is the strongest of all. In government, then, each member is first himself, then a magistrate, then a citizen — exactly the reverse of the order the social system requires.

Granting this, suppose the whole government is in the hands of one man. Then the particular will and the corporate will are wholly united, and so the corporate will is at the highest degree of intensity it can reach. But the use made of the force depends on the degree the will reaches, and the absolute force of the government does not vary. It follows that the most active government is that of one man.

Now suppose the opposite: we join the government to the legislative authority, make the Sovereign the prince as well, and make every citizen a magistrate. Then the corporate will, fused with the general will, can be no more active than that will, and it leaves the particular will as strong as it can possibly be. So the government, whose absolute force never changes, sits at the lowest point of its relative force or activity.

These relations are beyond question, and other considerations confirm them further. For instance, each magistrate is more active in his own body than each citizen is in his. So the particular will has far more influence on the acts of the government than on those of the Sovereign, because a magistrate is almost always charged with some governmental function, while no citizen, taken singly, exercises any function of Sovereignty. Furthermore, as the State grows bigger, its real force increases, though not in direct proportion to its growth. But if the State stays the same, the number of magistrates can increase without limit and the government gains no greater real force, since its force is the State’s, and the State’s size stays the same. So the relative force or activity of the government decreases, while its absolute or real force cannot increase.

Moreover, it is certain that promptness in carrying out business diminishes as more people are put in charge of it. Where too much is made of prudence, too little is made of fortune; opportunity is let slip, and deliberation causes the loss of its object.

I have just shown that the government grows slack as the number of magistrates increases, and I showed earlier that the more numerous the people, the greater the repressive force must be. It follows that the relation of the magistrates to the government should vary inversely to the relation of the subjects to the Sovereign. That is, the larger the State, the tighter its government should be, so that the number of rulers shrinks as the number of the people grows.

I should add that I am speaking here of the government’s relative strength, not of how upright it is. On that point the reverse holds: the more numerous the magistracy, the closer the corporate will comes to the general will, while under a single magistrate the corporate will is, as I said, merely a particular will. So what is gained on one side is lost on the other. The art of the legislator is to know where to set the point at which the force and the will of the government, which are always in inverse proportion, meet in the relation that serves the State best.
